Fastiv Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Fastiv, Ukraine

Not demolished. Fastiv's Jewish community's exact founding is unknown, likely destroyed if it existed during the 1648-49 Khmelnytsky Uprising; Jews are documented there from 1700. Avraam Malakh, son of Rabbi Dov Ber of Mezhirich, mentored the community from 1772-1776; Rabbi Israel Polotzker, one of Dov Ber's first students, died there in 1782 while passing through. The community suffered repeated Haidamak pogroms (1750, 1752, 1768) and later Denikin-era violence (1918-20); population grew from 2,694 (1847) to 5,595 by 1897. A separate Jewish agricultural settlement, Kadlubitsa, also endured 1918-19 Denikin pogroms, later rebuilt with JDC assistance, and hosted a Jewish collective farm ('Roiter Poyer') under Soviet collectivization. German occupation removed most adult Jews to Bila Tserkva, while a special ghetto held children separately; Kadlubitsa's residents, the children's ghetto population, and Jewish refugees from Zhytomyr were all massacred in a forest outside town, with some remains later reburied at this cemetery. An underground Jewish community persisted postwar through secret minyanim and informal cemetery-maintenance fundraising, formally re-registering in 1998. This cemetery, with tombstones dating from 1906, remains active today, with its most recent burial in 2008. One of Fastiv's original two Jewish cemeteries closed in the 19th century and was later earmarked for private construction; its exact location is now unknown.
